synopsis: The booklet recommends replacing single completion dates with program-model-derived P50 and P80 dates—50% and 80% chances of completion—and the probability of meeting the fixed deadline; its empirical warning includes a 1994 study in which only 29.7% finished by their best-estimate date [f205, f16310, f16320, f9599]. Reference class forecasting uses actual outcomes of comparable projects, but reported superiority over other methods depends on genuine similarity; Chapter 13 also says the Flyvbjerg literature was not verified, creating an internal evidence-status tension [f9604, f9606, f9609, f10743]. Documented validation-capability programs took years, including PEGASUS's 42 months and EVIDENT's approximately 33 months, while VaViM's six months delivered only a pre-study; the booklet therefore treats four months as a validation window, not a capability-construction window, and as a target rather than a forecast [f15713, f15694, f15710, f15709, f15714, f10464]. No reference class of first-time programs meeting that four-month window was found, and the manufacturer's internal three-to-four-year history was unavailable; reconstructing that history is recommended before claiming a tenfold schedule reduction, because the actual bottleneck remains unknown [f10465, f11287, f273, f10860, f11288]. For first-of-a-kind work, the recommendation is component-level historical reference classes, openly stated uplifts where data are thin, and schedule-risk analysis, although this decomposition is not a separately validated forecasting method [f9439, f9613, f9615, f9616, f16318]. The proposed March–April 2027 G2 gate requires a blind pilot meeting pre-set metrics, assessor feedback, and a P80 date inside the deadline; the executive brief should show preparation and delivery P50/P80 dates and descoping measures that preserve deadline confidence [f12306, f16323].
